description_medium: Trump commuted Anthony M. DeJohn’s federal sentence in January 2021 after he had served more than 13 years of a life term for a marijuana-distribution conspiracy. The White House statement said DeJohn had a clear disciplinary record, was recognized for his work ethic, and had employment and housing available upon release. DOJ lists his Northern District of New York case and a July 2010 sentence of life plus 10 years’ supervision; the precise amended terms are not stated.
description_long: The Justice Department records Anthony M. DeJohn among the people whose sentences Donald Trump commuted on January 19, 2021. It places his case in the Northern District of New York and lists life imprisonment plus 10 years of supervised release, imposed July 26, 2010, for a marijuana-distribution conspiracy and firearm possession by a convicted felon. A January 20 White House statement offered the administration’s rationale: DeJohn had served more than 13 years of the life sentence, maintained a clear disciplinary record, and earned recognition for his work ethic in prison. It also said he had employment and housing available on release. The public DOJ summary does not specify the exact replacement sentence or supervision terms. The official explanation describes the administration’s stated grounds for clemency, but is not independent evaluation of the case. The commutation altered punishment; it did not erase the convictions.
evidence_notes: Repository packet reviewed: The linked DOJ clemency list confirms the commutation entry, but the packet does not supply DeJohn’s offense, sentence, date-specific clemency instrument, or reason. Without those case details, a full explanation would require unsupported padding. Focused web research: DOJ’s official commutations list gives the original case details; the archived White House January 20, 2021 clemency statement states the administration’s recipient-specific rationale and release context. Exact amended terms are not specified in those public summaries.

description_medium: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump commuted Darrell Frazier’s federal sentences. DOJ lists two cases: a life sentence for a cocaine-conspiracy conviction in Tennessee and a consecutive 18-month sentence plus six years of supervised release for a heroin-conspiracy conviction in Georgia. The White House said he had served 29 years, maintained an exemplary prison record, and created a nonprofit tennis foundation serving children. The public entry does not state the replacement terms.
description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency list records Donald Trump’s January 19, 2021 commutation of Darrell Frazier’s federal sentences. It identifies two separate cases. In the Eastern District of Tennessee, Frazier received life imprisonment in 1990 for conspiring to distribute and possess cocaine hydrochloride. In the Northern District of Georgia, he received an 18-month consecutive term and six years of supervised release in 2004 for a heroin-conspiracy offense. A White House statement dated January 20 gave the administration’s stated rationale: Frazier had served 29 years of a life sentence, maintained an exemplary prison disciplinary record, and created a nonprofit foundation providing free tennis lessons to children in underserved communities. It also described planned employment and housing with his mother after release. DOJ confirms the original sentences and grant but does not give a revised term or supervision conditions. The two convictions remain distinct, and the commutation did not erase them.
evidence_notes: Repository packet reviewed: Read the linked DOJ commutations page. It identifies Frazier’s two federal cases, underlying offenses, original sentence terms, and the Jan. 19, 2021 clemency date, but does not give the commuted terms or a rationale. The source therefore supports a concise event account but not a full explanation of the practical effect. DOJ’s official list confirms the January 19, 2021 commutation, Frazier’s two federal cases, the original sentences and offenses. It does not give the commuted terms or a published rationale; the signed instrument or recipient-specific clemency statement is still needed to describe the practical change. Focused web research: DOJ’s official commutations list gives the original case details; the archived White House January 20, 2021 clemency statement states the administration’s recipient-specific rationale and release context. description_medium: Donald Trump commuted Traie Tavares Kelly’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. DOJ lists a South Carolina cocaine-conspiracy conviction and an original 240-month prison term plus 10 years of supervised release. The White House said Kelly had served over 14 years, would likely face a 10-year mandatory minimum under current law, and had substantial work, education, and programming records in prison. The stated rationale is not the substituted sentence; DOJ does not publish the amended terms here.
description_long: The Justice Department’s list records Donald Trump’s January 19, 2021 commutation of Traie Tavares Kelly’s federal sentence. It identifies a District of South Carolina conviction for conspiring to distribute at least 50 grams of cocaine base and at least five kilograms of cocaine. Kelly’s original sentence, imposed January 7, 2009, was 240 months in prison and 10 years of supervised release. In a January 20 statement, the White House said Kelly had served more than 14 years and would likely have faced only a 10-year mandatory minimum if sentenced under then-current law. It also cited his work history, education, and programming while incarcerated as evidence of preparation for productive citizenship after release. These are the administration’s stated reasons for clemency. The public DOJ page does not identify the exact replacement term or supervision conditions, so the practical sentence change cannot be specified from that summary. The action commuted punishment without vacating the conviction.
evidence_notes: Repository packet reviewed: The Justice Department list supports the offense, district, original 240-month sentence, and 10 years of supervised release. It does not give the amended terms or a rationale, and it supplies no evidence for the “Corrupt Pardons” characterization. A focused read of the Justice Department entry confirms the South Carolina conviction and original 240-month term plus 10 years of supervised release imposed January 7, 2009. It does not state the substituted sentence or explain why Trump selected Kelly. The missing evidence is the commutation instrument or another official record giving the amended terms and rationale; there is also no evidence in the linked record for the “Corrupt Pardons” subcategory. Focused web research: DOJ’s official commutations list gives the original case details; the archived White House January 20, 2021 clemency statement states the administration’s recipient-specific rationale and release context. Exact amended terms are not specified in those public summaries.

description_medium: On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump commuted Ferrell Damon Scott’s federal sentence. DOJ lists a Texas marijuana case with an original life term, 10 years of supervised release, and a $10,000 fine. The White House said Scott had served nearly nine years; his former prosecutor strongly opposed a mandatory life sentence, arguing today’s guidelines likely would produce a less severe punishment. The public clemency listing does not state the substituted sentence or whether other penalties changed.
description_long: Donald Trump commuted Ferrell Damon Scott’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. The Justice Department places the case in the Southern District of Texas and describes a conspiracy involving more than 1,000 kilograms of marijuana, with three additional counts involving more than 100 kilograms. Scott’s original sentence, imposed April 2, 2009, included life imprisonment, 10 years of supervised release, and a $10,000 fine. The White House’s January 20 statement said Scott had served nearly nine years and cited support from former acting U.S. Attorney Sam Sheldon, who had prosecuted the case and argued that Scott did not deserve a mandatory life sentence. The statement added that under then-current sentencing guidelines Scott likely would not have received so severe a sentence. These were the administration’s stated grounds for clemency. DOJ’s public list does not specify the replacement prison term or whether supervision and the fine remained in force. The commutation changed punishment but did not itself vacate the conviction.
evidence_notes: Repository packet reviewed: The Justice Department list supports the underlying offenses and original life sentence, supervised release, and fine. It omits the amended terms and gives no rationale or evidence for the “Corrupt Pardons” characterization. The DOJ list supports the commutation and the original offenses and sentence, but it does not provide the substituted sentence, whether supervised release or the fine changed, or a rationale. The record also contains no evidence of favoritism or exchange to support “Corrupt Pardons.” The amended clemency order and documented grounds are needed. Focused web research: DOJ’s official commutations list gives the original case details; the archived White House January 20, 2021 clemency statement states the administration’s recipient-specific rationale and release context. Exact amended terms are not specified in those public summaries.

description_medium: On March 23, 2017, the General Services Administration found Trump Old Post Office LLC in compliance with its lease for the Washington building that housed the Trump International Hotel. A later GSA inspector-general evaluation said the agency had declined to address constitutional emoluments questions that could bear on the lease, affecting its Section 37.19 analysis. The IG did not decide whether Trump’s interest violated the Constitution or lease.
description_long: The General Services Administration’s March 23, 2017 determination found Trump Old Post Office LLC in compliance with Section 37.19 of its lease for the government-owned Old Post Office building, where the Trump International Hotel operated. The lease restricted elected officials’ participation in the tenant arrangement. A later evaluation by GSA’s inspector general examined how the agency reached that conclusion. The IG said GSA recognized that President Trump’s business interest raised possible issues under the Foreign and Presidential Emoluments Clauses but chose not to address them. According to the evaluation, omitting those constitutional questions affected GSA’s Section 37.19 analysis and left uncertainty unresolved. The IG did not determine that Trump’s interest violated either constitutional clause or that a violation caused a lease breach; it assessed GSA’s process. The episode therefore includes both the agency’s compliance finding and an official critique of the scope of its review.
evidence_notes: Repository packet reviewed: Needs context: the supplied linked pages are general GSA references, not documentation of the March 23, 2017 lease determination. The record lacks the agency statement, lease terms or compliance rationale needed for an accurate long explanation. Focused primary-source review: the GSA FOIA library links the March 23, 2017 contracting officer letter; the GSA OIG release says GSA certified compliance with Section 37.19 after excluding emoluments issues and that the evaluation did not decide whether any constitutional or lease violation occurred.
